newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices soar as freeze hits young U.S. crop.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices soar as freeze hits young U.S. crop.

text.p: Wheat prices soared on Monday after freezing temperatures clamped down on the developing winter wheat crop in the United States, threatening to cut both production and exports this year, analysts said.

"This is a major event," said Charlie Sernatinger, director of commodity operations at Man International, who estimated 100 to 150 million bushels, or about three to four million metric tons, of wheat were lost when freezing temperatures swept from Kansas to Texas.
"This is two million tons of exportable wheat we cannot afford to lose," he said, referring to the portion of the damaged crop that would likely have been sold overseas.

That message was not lost on futures traders, who just over a year ago sent wheat prices to a record high of $7.50 a bushel on similar worries about the U.S. crop. At that time, world grain stocks were at 20-year lows.

On Monday, wheat for May delivery at the Chicago Board of Trade jumped the 20-cent-per-bushel daily trading limit at the opening bell and stayed there. May wheat closed at $4.23, up 20 cents a bushel.
At the Kansas City Board of Trade, May wheat also ended locked up the daily 25-cent limit at $4.76-1/2.
Kansas State University wheat breeder Rollie Sears estimated a 40 percent production loss in southern Kansas, an area that produced 40 percent of the state's wheat last year.
Kansas alone produces 10 to 20 percent of the U.S. wheat crop which totals about 2.3 billion bushels.
"We had a good crop and basically the potential for a good crop is out the window," Sears said. "Right now it is pretty depressing."

Temperatures dipped into the teens Fahrenheit over the weekend from Kansas into Oklahoma and the Texas panhandle. Another cold spell was forecast overnight Monday although temperatures were not expected to match the weekend lows.
"It looks to be a very serious event in terms of loss of production in the central Plains winter wheat crop," said Joel Burgio, a meteorologist for Weather Services Corp.
"The damage occurred on Saturday and Sunday. We had a very serious freeze on those two mornings," he said.

As the freeze hit, world wheat supplies remained tight. The U.S. Agriculture Department on April 11 estimated world wheat stocks at 108.3 million metric tons by July, down from 112.2 million estimated a month earlier.
World wheat consumption is expected to rise to 579 million tons this year from 552 million a year ago.

With Monday's gains, wheat prices have risen 14 percent since April 4. Traders were already worried about flooding in the Dakotas and Minnesota, the heart of the U.S. spring wheat belt, which is now bound to see planting delays.
Acreage planted to hard red winter wheat from Kansas to Texas was already down five percent this year at 34.1 million acres as many farmers planned on planting high-priced crops like soybeans.
Recent dry weather has reduced crop prospects for Australia and France, two of the top five wheat exporters.
Sernatinger said the freeze, coupled with an expected smaller U.S. spring wheat crop and overseas crop problems, could easily push U.S. prices near $5 a bushel soon.
U.S. wheat prices last surpassed $5 in July 1996 as dry weather from Kansas to Texas hurt production.
Prior to the freeze, Kansas wheat was developing well and some analysts expected a state crop near 400 million bushels, the largest since the 1993 harvest of 433 million.
Kansas farmers harvested 255.2 million bushels in 1996.
"If we could have favorable weather late into spring, that would minimize the damage," T.J. Byram, state statistician for the Kansas Agriculture Statistics Service, said on Monday.
